routines.deleteDayConfirmation: This will remove all sets, exercises and progression rules
routines.fitDaysInWeekHelpText: This setting controls how your routine's days are scheduled across multiple weeks. If enabled, the days will repeat in a weekly cycle. For example, a routine with workouts on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday will continue this pattern on the following Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. If disabled, the days will follow sequentially without regard to the start of a new week. This is useful for routines that don't follow a strict weekly schedule.
routines.needsLogsToAdvanceHelpText: If you select this option, the routine will only progress to the next scheduled day if you've logged a workout for the current day. If this option is not selected, the routine will automatically advance to the next day regardless of whether you logged a workout or not.

routines.roundingHelp: Set the default rounding for weight and repetitions (this is specially useful when using the percentage increase step in the progression). This will apply to all new sets but can be changed individually in the progression form. Leave empty to disable rounding.
routines.weightLogNotPlanned: Saving logs to a date for which no workouts were planned.

routines.confirmRestDayHelpText: Please note that all sets and exercises will be removed when you mark a day as a rest day.
routines.impressionHelpText: This form records your workout results (reps, weight, etc.) for each exercise. Changes you make here, like removing or swapping exercises, only affect the specific logs you save and and won't change your overall routine. Only rows with values for either weight or repetitions are saved.

routines.templatesHelpText: Templates are a way to save your routine for later use and as a starting point for further routines. You can't edit templates, but you can duplicate them and make changes to the copy (as well as converting them back to a regular routine, of course).

oneRm.name: One-repetition maximum
oneRm.what: The heaviest weight you can lift for a single clean repetition. It is usually estimated from a set of several repetitions instead of being tested all-out.
oneRm.how: It lets you compare strength over time and pick working weights as a percentage of it, so your training stays hard enough to make you stronger without guessing.
oneRm.example: You lift 80 kg for 5 repetitions, which is an estimated 1RM of about 93 kg. Working sets at 70% of it are around 65 kg.

rir.name: Repetitions in reserve
rir.what: How many more repetitions you could still have done with good form when you stop a set.
rir.how: It keeps the effort of every set under control: close to failure builds muscle and strength, while leaving a reserve protects your joints and your recovery.
rir.example: RIR 2 means you stop the set while you could have done 2 more repetitions.

rpe.name: Rating of perceived exertion
rpe.what: A scale from 1 to 10 for how hard a set felt. 10 is the most you could do, 8 means about 2 repetitions were left.
rpe.how: It lets you adjust the load by feel on days when you are tired or fresh, so the effort stays on target.
rpe.example: A set planned at RPE 8 that felt like a 10 tells you to lower the weight next time.

doubleProgression.name: Double progression
doubleProgression.what: A way to progress with a repetition range. You first add repetitions until you reach the top of the range in all sets, then you add weight and start at the bottom of the range again.
doubleProgression.how: It gives you a clear rule for when to go heavier and makes progress steady, with no need to jump weight before you are ready.
doubleProgression.example: With 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions: when you manage 12, 12, 12 at 40 kg, next time use 42.5 kg and aim for 8 again.

deload.name: Deload week
deload.what: A planned lighter week, with less weight or fewer sets, so the body can recover from accumulated fatigue.
deload.how: It lowers the risk of overtraining and injury and often lets you come back stronger after it.
deload.example: After 8 weeks of progression, week 9 uses 60% of the usual weight and half of the sets.

superset.name: Superset
superset.what: Two or more exercises done back to back with little or no rest in between, and rest only after the last one.
superset.how: It saves time and raises the intensity of a session, which is useful when your time is limited.
superset.example: Biceps curls followed straight away by triceps extensions, then 90 seconds of rest.

amrap.name: As many repetitions as possible
amrap.what: A set where you do as many repetitions as you can, or as many rounds as you can in a given time.
amrap.how: It shows your current capacity and gives a number to beat next time, which makes progress easy to see.
amrap.example: AMRAP of push-ups with your own body weight: you stop at 23, and next time you aim for 24.

pr.name: Personal record
pr.what: Your best result so far in an exercise: the most weight, the most repetitions or the best time.
pr.how: Records are a clear and motivating sign that your plan works, and they mark the points to build on.
pr.example: Bench press 60 kg for 8 repetitions, where your best was 7: that is a repetition PR at 60 kg.

volume.name: Training volume
volume.what: The total amount of work you do, usually counted as sets, or as sets times repetitions times weight.
volume.how: Volume is one of the main drivers of muscle growth. Tracking it helps you increase the workload gradually and notice when it is too much or too little.
volume.example: 3 sets of 10 repetitions at 50 kg is 1,500 kg of volume for that exercise.

kcal.name: Kilocalories
kcal.what: The unit for the energy in food and the energy your body uses. What people call calories on a label is kcal.
kcal.how: Eating fewer kcal than you use leads to weight loss, more leads to weight gain. Knowing your target makes the plan to reach your goal concrete.
kcal.example: A target of 2,200 kcal per day to keep your weight, or about 1,900 kcal to lose weight slowly.

macros.name: Macronutrients
macros.what: The three groups of nutrients that provide energy: protein, carbohydrates and fat.
macros.how: Enough protein supports muscle, carbohydrates fuel training and fat supports hormones, so a good split makes your kcal work for your goal.
macros.example: A day with 150 g of protein, 250 g of carbohydrates and 70 g of fat is about 2,230 kcal.

nutriScore.name: Nutri-Score
nutriScore.what: A label from A (green) to E (red) that rates the overall nutritional quality of a food, mainly by comparing sugar, salt and saturated fat with fibre and protein.
nutriScore.how: It is a quick way to compare similar products when you shop and to choose the better one for your diet.
nutriScore.example: Between two breakfast cereals, the one with a B is a better everyday choice than the one with a D.

nova.name: NOVA classification
nova.what: A grouping of foods from 1 to 4 by how much they are processed: 1 is unprocessed or minimally processed, 4 is ultra-processed.
nova.how: Building most of your meals from groups 1 and 2 makes it easier to eat well and to feel full on fewer kcal.
nova.example: An apple is NOVA 1, a pack of sweet biscuits is NOVA 4.

movingAverage.name: 7-day moving average
movingAverage.what: The average of the last 7 days, recalculated every day. It smooths out the daily ups and downs.
movingAverage.how: Body weight changes by up to 1 to 2 kg from day to day because of water and food. The average shows the real trend, so you do not react to noise.
movingAverage.example: Weights of 81.2, 80.6, 81.5, 80.9, 81.0, 80.7 and 81.1 kg give a 7-day average of 81.0 kg.

hr.name: Heart rate
hr.what: How many times your heart beats per minute (bpm).
hr.how: It tells you how hard your body is working, so you can train in the zone that fits your goal, easy for endurance and recovery, hard for intervals.
hr.example: A resting HR of 60 bpm, and 150 bpm during a run, where your maximum is about 190 bpm.

stepsPerMinute.name: Steps per minute
stepsPerMinute.what: Your walking or running cadence: how many steps you take in a minute.
stepsPerMinute.how: It is an easy way to check the intensity of a walk. Moderate intensity starts at around 100 steps per minute, a brisk pace at around 130.
stepsPerMinute.example: A 30 minute walk at 110 steps per minute is 3,300 steps at moderate intensity.

bpm.name: Beats per minute
bpm.what: The tempo of a song. In training music, a higher BPM feels more energetic.
bpm.how: Music at the tempo of your activity helps you keep rhythm and effort: slower for warm-up and recovery, faster for intervals.
bpm.example: Around 100 to 120 BPM for a warm-up, 120 to 140 for strength work, 150 to 170 for high-intensity intervals.
